issues.legal_issue: A Hindu family that remains undivided is within the statutory description of a Hindu undivided family even when it is governed by a matrilineal customary system rather than the Mitakshara system.
material_facts: The family consisted of Hindus and remained undivided, although its members had agreed to the separate enjoyment of some family properties.
The family was governed by a matrilineal customary system in which descent was traced through females and male and female members had equal rights in family property.
The family’s karta filed an expenditure-tax return in the status of a Hindu undivided family.
issues.conclusion: The family fell within the expression “Hindu undivided family” in the charging provision, despite the differences between its customary system and the Mitakshara system.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3(1) of the Expenditure-tax Act charged tax on expenditure incurred by an individual or a Hindu undivided family. The Court held that a Hindu family governed by a matrilineal customary system remained a Hindu undivided family for this purpose, notwithstanding its distinct rules of descent and property rights.

predicates.expenditure_tax_assessment: The matter concerns an assessment of expenditure tax on family expenditure.
predicates.undivided_family: The family remains undivided, even if its members separately enjoy some family property.

issues.definition: When an expenditure-tax assessment concerns a Hindu family that remains undivided, the family is treated as a taxable family unit.

issues.legal_issue: Treating a Hindu undivided family governed by a matrilineal customary system as a unit of expenditure taxation, while treating a non-Hindu family governed by a similar system as an individual, does not necessarily deny equal protection.
material_facts: The family was assessed as a Hindu undivided family, and the expenditure incurred by its different members was aggregated.
A non-Hindu family governed by a broadly similar matrilineal system was treated as an individual for tax purposes and could therefore face a lower rate of tax.

Although the two family systems shared female-line descent and community of interest in family property, their laws differed in other respects, including property relations and the effects of marriage and inheritance rules.
The non-Hindu community was small, geographically limited, and dwindling.
Legislation had long treated Hindu undivided families as a distinct taxable class and had treated the relevant non-Hindu families as individuals.
issues.conclusion: The distinction did not create an obvious inequality or discrimination contrary to Article 14, and the charging provision was not invalid on that ground.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits substantial legislative discretion in classifying subjects of taxation. A taxing law may use different tax units, methods, or rates where the classification is rational; it violates Article 14 if it imposes an obviously unequal incidence of taxation on persons or things similarly situated. The legislature need not tax every possible class. The Court relied on Raja Jagannath Baksh Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh and Another, [1963] 1 S.C.R. 220, and applied these principles to section 3(1) of the Expenditure-tax Act.

predicates.constitutional_challenge_to_taxing_class: A party challenges a tax classification on the ground that it denies equal protection.
predicates.hindu_family_unit_taxed_on_combined_expe: A Hindu undivided family is treated as a tax unit and the expenditure of its members is combined.
predicates.comparable_non_hindu_family_taxed_as_ind: A non-Hindu family with some comparable customary features is treated as an individual for tax purposes.
predicates.family_systems_differ_in_material_proper: The two family systems share some characteristics but differ in material rules governing family property or succession.
predicates.excluded_group_is_small_and_limited: The excluded group is small and confined to a limited area.
predicates.tax_law_history_distinguishes_hindu_fami: A longstanding pattern of tax legislation treats Hindu undivided families as a distinct class from the relevant non-Hindu families.

issues.definition: If a tax-classification challenge involves combined taxation of Hindu family expenditure and individual taxation of a comparable non-Hindu family, and the family systems materially differ, the excluded group is small and limited, and tax law has long distinguished the classes, the classification survives the equal-protection challenge.
